strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: reducing the substantial critic-related cost of end-to-end reinforcement learning for LLM-based multi-agent systems.
The three rollout strategies—Independent Sampling, Fork-on-first, and Round-robin—provide an intuitive design space for balancing homogeneous comparisons, cross-agent coordination, and rollout cost.

The empirical study includes in-domain HotpotQA results, transfer to 2WikiMultiHopQA and MuSiQue, training curves, behavioral analyses of individual agents, and hardware-efficiency measurements. FoF and RR improve over the reported MAPPO point estimates on most metrics while using less memory.
Prompts, agent-specific penalties, core hyperparameters, and pseudocode are provided, and the case study usefully illustrates how reinforcement learning changes retrieval behavior.
The presentation is generally readable, with figures that make the multi-agent sampling schemes and training dynamics accessible.
weaknesses: The formal method is internally inconsistent. Equations 1, 6, and 7 use the reference policy as the importance-sampling denominator, whereas PPO/GRPO normally use a frozen old behavior policy and employ the reference model separately for KL regularization. The paper does not clarify whether this is merely incorrect notation or the algorithm actually implemented.

The group-identifier pseudocode appears to contradict the central method. Algorithm 2 assigns one identifier to every agent output within a single trajectory. Equation 5 would therefore compare different agent roles along that trajectory, whereas the prose and figures describe comparing the G outputs of a given agent across trajectories. This ambiguity affects what MHGPO actually optimizes and prevents faithful reproduction.

The treatment of token-level credit is unclear and potentially consequential. The paper states that reward is assigned only to the last token and then uses token-wise advantages in Equation 6. If only the final token receives a nonzero advantage, the objective cannot directly train most generated content; standard GRPO instead broadcasts a sequence-level advantage across completion tokens. The reported learning curves suggest that the implementation may differ from the written method.

The evaluation does not establish statistical reliability. Only point estimates from apparently one training run are reported, without random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several improvements over MAPPO are small, and performance is not uniformly better: for example, MHGPO-IS is worse than MAPPO across the reported transfer results, while RR loses to MAPPO on MuSiQue accuracy.

The paper repeatedly evaluates on the first 500 examples of the HotpotQA test set during training and then reports HotpotQA test performance. It is unclear whether the final test table includes those same examples or whether “test” actually denotes a validation split. Repeated model selection on test examples would constitute leakage, and the split protocol must be corrected or precisely documented.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the appendix. There is no code or model-release statement, and essential details are missing: exact Wikipedia dump and indexing procedure, retrieval depth and Contriever configuration, decoding parameters, random seeds, evaluation-set sizes, checkpoint-selection rule, PPO critic/value-loss settings, optimizer and schedule, gradient/minibatch details, and the mapping of the two listed learning rates to methods.

The central causal claims are weakly isolated. There are no ablations of group size, RR probabilities, reward propagation, format penalties, or heterogeneous versus randomly regrouped advantages, and no straightforward critic-free trajectory-level GRPO/REINFORCE baseline. Consequently, the gains cannot confidently be attributed to heterogeneous grouping rather than implementation or tuning differences.

The scope of evidence is narrow: one 8B backbone, one fixed three-agent linear search architecture, one training dataset, and one epoch. This does not support claims that the method applies to general multi-agent systems, nor does it establish stability beyond a single run. Efficiency is also reported as GPU-memory percentages and partial timing components rather than reproducible peak memory and end-to-end throughput.

There are additional technical and scholarly inaccuracies: GRPO is incorrectly attributed to Schulman et al. (2016), which is the GAE paper; PPO and MAPPO are used inconsistently; “Accuracy” is described as normalized answer overlap without a precise definition; and the unusually large discrepancy between exact match and F1 for the single-LLM RL baseline is not investigated. These issues further reduce confidence in the implementation and comparisons.

Overall, the idea is promising and the reported results motivate further study, but the algorithmic contradictions, possible evaluation leakage, absent uncertainty estimates, and incomplete reproduction details currently prevent a sound Findings recommendation. A revision could plausibly be ready for a subsequent cycle if it reconciles the equations and pseudocode with released implementation, uses a clean held-out protocol, and adds controlled multi-seed ablations.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: reducing the cost and instability of reinforcement learning for LLM-based multi-agent systems. Replacing an 8B-parameter critic with group-relative advantage estimates is practically motivated.

MHGPO is presented as a reasonably coherent framework combining shared-parameter agents, terminal-reward propagation, and three rollout/grouping strategies. The appendix provides pseudocode and full agent prompts.

The empirical results show promising gains for FoF and RR over the reported MAPPO baseline. On HotpotQA, RR improves F1 from 46.400 to 49.724, while FoF and RR also generally transfer better to 2WikiMultiHopQA and MuSiQue.

The resource measurements support the limited claim that eliminating the critic reduces memory and training time in the evaluated implementation. The paper also includes useful training-curve, behavioral, and qualitative analyses.
The work is clearly relevant to NLP, particularly retrieval-augmented generation, multi-hop question answering, and reinforcement learning for LLM agents.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is not rigorous enough to establish the central superiority and stability claims. Results appear to come from one run with one 8B backbone, one training dataset, and one three-agent pipeline. There are no random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; consequently, modest differences such as RR versus FoF or MHGPO versus MAPPO on 2WikiMultiHopQA cannot be interpreted reliably.

The algorithm specification contains a serious inconsistency. Algorithm 2 assigns one group identifier to all agent outputs within each trajectory, whereas the prose and figures describe grouping outputs across trajectories at a given agent. These definitions produce materially different advantage estimates, so the implemented method cannot be reconstructed confidently from the paper.

The policy objective is underspecified and possibly incorrect as written. Equations 1, 6, and 7 use the fixed reference policy both as the rollout distribution and as the denominator of the PPO importance ratio, without defining a distinct behavior/old policy or explaining when the reference is updated. This differs from standard PPO/GRPO implementations and leaves the actual optimization procedure unclear. Numerical handling of zero within-group reward variance is also unspecified.

The evaluation lacks essential ablations. It does not isolate the effects of heterogeneous grouping, backward reward propagation, parameter sharing, or agent-specific penalties; examine group size or RR sampling probabilities; or compare against a straightforward per-agent/shared-model GRPO baseline. Thus, the results do not establish that heterogeneous groups, rather than other design choices, cause the improvements.

The claimed explanation for why heterogeneous grouping works is speculative. Increasing output-level F1 similarity does not show that prompts, retrieved evidence, reward distributions, or induced learning problems become homogeneous, and no causal experiment tests this account.

The paper overgeneralizes from a single linear retrieval-QA workflow with three roles, a shared Llama-3.1-8B model, and answer-F1 rewards to general multi-agent systems. It provides no evidence for heterogeneous backbones, branching or cyclic communication, dynamic agent routing, non-QA tasks, or rewards that cannot be propagated through a simple chain.

Dataset protocol is ambiguous and potentially problematic: the paper says that validation repeatedly uses the first 500 samples of the 'test set,' but does not clearly identify official splits, sample counts for final evaluations, or whether this repeated evaluation influenced model or hyperparameter selection. The definition of Accuracy is also unclear, and the anomalous 0.500 EM versus 27.421 F1 for the single-LLM RL baseline is not investigated.

The MAPPO comparison is insufficiently controlled and documented. There is no hyperparameter search description, seed-level comparison, evidence that both methods received comparable tuning or environment interactions, or analysis of alternative smaller critics. The memory advantage is largely expected from deleting an 8B critic and does not by itself demonstrate a generally better learning algorithm.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code or artifact link is given, and important details such as decoding parameters, maximum lengths, optimizer and schedule, gradient settings, exact learning-rate assignment, retrieval-corpus snapshot and indexing, checkpoint selection, KL computation, and evaluation normalization are absent.

Several presentation and scholarship issues reduce confidence, including inconsistent use of PPO versus MAPPO, calling GRPO a Schulman et al. (2016) method, describing DeepSeekMath as DeepSeek-R1, unsupported use of 'significant,' and claims of consistent superiority even though MHGPO-IS is worse than MAPPO across all reported datasets. The contribution is promising, but substantial methodological clarification and stronger controlled experiments are required before it meets the soundness and reproducibility bar for Findings.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practically important NLP problem: end-to-end reinforcement learning for LLM-based multi-agent retrieval and question-answering systems.

The critic-free formulation is well motivated. Avoiding an actor-sized critic plausibly reduces memory and computation, and the reported measurements show substantial savings relative to the implemented MAPPO baseline.

The three sampling strategies—Independent Sampling, Fork-on-first, and Round-robin—provide a useful exploration of efficiency versus grouping structure. FoF and RR outperform MAPPO on most reported metrics, with especially clear gains on in-domain HotpotQA.

The evaluation covers a complete three-agent pipeline rather than isolated components, and transfer results on 2WikiMultiHopQA and MuSiQue provide some evidence that the learned policy is not entirely specific to the training set.

The behavior analyses, efficiency breakdown, training curves, agent-level statistics, and qualitative example help illuminate how optimization changes the system. The manuscript is generally readable and visually clear.
weaknesses: The evidence is based on one backbone, one three-agent architecture, one training dataset, and apparently one run per condition. There are no results over random seeds, uncertainty estimates for task performance, or significance tests. Consequently, the modest differences between MHGPO and MAPPO—particularly out of domain—do not establish consistent superiority or greater stability.

The validation protocol uses the first 500 examples of the HotpotQA test set every five training steps. This repeatedly exposes test examples during development and potentially model or checkpoint selection, compromising the claimed held-out test evaluation unless the authors can demonstrate that these observations influenced no decisions.

There are consequential inconsistencies in the method specification. Algorithm 2 assigns each trajectory index as the group identifier for every agent output in that trajectory, which appears to group different agents within one trajectory; the prose and figures instead describe grouping the G outputs of a given downstream agent across trajectories. Likewise, the text assigns reward only to the final token but does not explain how Equation 5 avoids zero-variance advantages for preceding tokens or whether the sequence-level advantage is broadcast. The PPO/GRPO importance ratio also conflates the rollout/old policy with the fixed reference policy. These ambiguities prevent reliable implementation and verification of the central method.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code or artifact is identified; decoding settings and retrieval configuration are incomplete; dataset evaluation sizes are absent; the definition of Accuracy is unclear; two learning rates are listed without mapping them to experiments; the answer-length penalty threshold is unspecified; and MAPPO tuning, critic training, and checkpoint-selection details are missing.

The baseline comparison does not isolate the source of the gains. In particular, there is no standard critic-free GRPO-style baseline with a straightforward grouping construction, no ablation of reward propagation or heterogeneous grouping under matched rollout budgets, and no stronger or alternative MAPPO critic configuration. The MAPPO baseline is trained without warm-up, making its observed instability an insufficient basis for a general claim about critic-based MARL.

The explanation for why heterogeneous grouping works remains speculative. Rising lexical F1 similarity does not show that heterogeneous advantage normalization is unbiased or preferable, nor does it establish that downstream prompts or retrieved evidence have become equivalent. Controlled ablations comparing homogeneous and heterogeneous groups at equal cost are needed.

Claims of applicability to general multi-agent systems and of being the first systematic investigation are broader than the evidence supports. All experiments concern a fixed, sequential, parameter-sharing retrieval-QA pipeline; systems with branching communication, non-shared policies, different rewards, or other NLP tasks are not evaluated. Overall, the idea is promising, but resolving the evaluation leakage, algorithmic ambiguities, and missing statistical/reproducibility evidence is necessary before a Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem: efficiently optimizing tool-using, multi-agent LLM systems from system-level rewards without maintaining a large critic.

MHGPO is intuitively motivated, and the Fork-on-first and Round-robin sampling strategies expose a useful efficiency-versus-local-comparability tradeoff. Parameter sharing and critic-free optimization are practically attractive.

The empirical study is reasonably broad for its setting: it compares against MAPPO, unoptimized multi-agent systems, and single-context search/RL systems; reports in-domain and out-of-domain QA results; and includes role, reward, aggregation, and group-size ablations.

The reported gains over MAPPO are meaningful on HotpotQA, while the memory and runtime measurements support the narrower claim that removing the critic reduces training cost. The authors also appropriately acknowledge limitations concerning task scope, model scale, agent topology, and the absence of a variance analysis.
weaknesses: The central algorithm is specified inconsistently. Algorithm 5 assigns the same group identifier to all agent outputs within trajectory i, whereas the method description and Proposition 3 require grouping outputs by agent across the G trajectories. Algorithm 3 additionally shuffles all singleton rollout pairs together without explicitly preserving agent role, despite the text describing role-specific groups. These differences change the advantages being optimized and prevent faithful reproduction of the claimed method.

The evidence does not isolate the claimed benefit of heterogeneous grouping. IS, FoF, RR, and FoF(os) differ simultaneously in group composition, branching location, rollout allocation, number of sampled completions, and compute. The role-freezing ablation shows that jointly training roles helps, but it does not demonstrate that heterogeneous normalization captures implicit cross-trajectory correlations. A controlled comparison holding trajectories and compute fixed while varying only the normalization groups is needed.

The theoretical result is considerably weaker than the presentation suggests. Under parameter sharing, deterministic prompt construction, the strong context-sufficiency assumption, identical reward broadcasting, and identical per-agent grouping, equality of token probabilities and surrogate terms is largely definitional. It is not equivalence to ordinary GRPO over complete-transcript returns unless that method is modified to use the same segment-wise groups. More importantly, the theory provides no guarantee for the incomplete-context regime in which MHGPO is claimed to be especially useful; the assertion that heterogeneous grouping solves coordination there remains heuristic.

Heterogeneous advantage estimates confound an agent's action quality with the quality of its rollout-specific upstream context. This may train downstream agents mainly on easier trajectories rather than provide valid credit assignment. The paper acknowledges the variance issue but supplies neither a formal analysis nor a diagnostic experiment that distinguishes beneficial coordination from this selection effect or from entropy collapse.

Statistical support for the principal conclusions is inadequate. The main benchmark table and learning curves provide no uncertainty estimates or stated number of seeds, even though several differences among MHGPO variants are small. Three-seed results are reported only for selected ablations. Evaluation-set sizes and significance tests are also absent.

Important reproducibility and evaluation details are missing or ambiguous, including decoding settings, optimizer and PPO-epoch configuration, retrieval depth and corpus snapshot, document construction, exact split/sample sizes, and a precise definition of the nonstandard Accuracy metric. Calling the labeled HotpotQA evaluation a test set is also ambiguous because official test labels are not publicly available. No code or complete executable configuration is identified.

Efficiency comparisons need tighter controls and clearer reporting. GPU memory is given as a percentage rather than peak allocated memory, timing combines rollout and optimization workloads that differ across sampling strategies, and it is unclear whether all methods receive matched environment interactions, generated tokens, or total compute. Thus the critic-memory advantage is credible, but broader claims of superior computational efficiency are not yet fully established.

Overall, the idea and preliminary results are promising, but the algorithmic inconsistency, insufficiently controlled evidence for the central mechanism, and incomplete reproducibility prevent a clear Findings recommendation in the current form. These concerns appear addressable in a substantial revision rather than requiring reconstruction of the entire work.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: reducing the cost of end-to-end reinforcement learning for multi-agent retrieval and QA systems.
The proposed critic-free framework is intuitively motivated, and the paper explores several rollout strategies with explicit efficiency trade-offs.

The empirical section reports task results on three QA datasets, training-time and memory measurements, role-wise ablations, reward-aggregation ablations, group-size sensitivity, and some multi-seed results.

The shared-backbone setup, agent prompts, reward propagation, and agent-specific formatting rewards are described more thoroughly than in many agent-training papers. The presentation and figures are generally clear.
weaknesses: The published algorithms are inconsistent with the central grouping mechanism. Algorithm 5 assigns the same group identifier to all agent outputs within one trajectory and different identifiers across the G trajectories. The prose and theoretical analysis instead require grouping a fixed agent's outputs across trajectories. As written, FoF would create groups of agent roles within a trajectory, while IS would leave singleton groups, making Equation 5 undefined. Algorithm 3 can additionally regroup singleton outputs without preserving role or root-question identity. This is a major soundness and reproducibility problem, not a cosmetic notation issue.

The evidence does not isolate the claimed benefit of heterogeneous grouping. IS, FoF, RR, and FoF(os) use different rollout structures, numbers of generated samples, and training-input distributions. There is no matched-compute baseline using the same trajectories and terminal rewards but conventional trajectory-level or homogeneous advantage estimation. Consequently, the reported gains cannot confidently be attributed to the proposed grouping operation.

Heterogeneous normalization confounds action quality with upstream-prefix difficulty. A downstream action can receive a low advantage because an upstream agent supplied a poor context, regardless of whether the downstream action was locally good. The paper calls this global coordination, but provides neither a causal credit-assignment analysis nor a comparison against appropriate counterfactual or leave-one-out estimators.

Backward reward propagation is essentially terminal-reward broadcasting and averaging over branches. The paper overstates this as demonstrating that indirect dependencies are captured. The role-freezing and single-role experiments only show that joint training is useful; they do not establish that the proposed estimator models inter-agent interactions better than simpler joint-policy training.

The theoretical result is weak and partly circular. Context sufficiency directly assumes equality between the local-prompt and full-transcript conditional distributions, after which probability and gradient equivalence follow immediately. Proposition 3 further defines the transcript baseline to use the same per-agent grouping as MHGPO, so it does not establish equivalence to ordinary GRPO over complete transcripts or justify the method when the assumption is violated—the regime in which the paper claims its main advantage.

The main results are reported without uncertainty or significance tests, despite relatively modest differences from MAPPO and among MHGPO variants. Multi-seed statistics appear only for selected ablations. Claims of consistent out-of-domain superiority are also stronger than the table supports: some variants lose to MAPPO on individual MuSiQue metrics.

Baseline attribution and efficiency comparisons need tighter controls. MAPPO uses an entire 8B critic, making its memory disadvantage expected, while alternative critic-free estimators are not compared under matched rollout budgets. GPU-memory percentages lack a precise definition, and end-to-end retrieval, rollout, and optimization costs are not sufficiently standardized for a scalability conclusion.

Reproduction would require substantial missing information, including the exact Wikipedia dump, retrieval top-k and snippet construction, decoding settings, optimizer and scheduler details, PPO epochs, maximum sequence lengths, exact agent-penalty thresholds, evaluation-set sizes, seed protocol, checkpoint selection, and code or configuration availability. The definition of “Accuracy” is also unclear and is described inconsistently as token-level accuracy versus normalized answer-hit.

The evaluation is limited to one 8B backbone, a fixed linear three-agent pipeline, and closely related multi-hop QA datasets. It therefore does not support the broader claims about general multi-agent systems, larger teams, non-linear coordination, or practical scalability. Overall, the idea is potentially useful, but the algorithmic contradiction and absence of attribution-quality controls prevent a Findings-level soundness recommendation in its current form.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: efficiently optimizing tool-using, multi-agent RAG systems under a system-level reward. The critic-free formulation is practically motivated and clearly distinguished from actor-critic MAPPO.

MHGPO combines shared-parameter training, backward terminal-reward propagation, and group-relative optimization in a coherent framework. The FoF, RR, and oversampling variants expose useful trade-offs between rollout cost, homogeneous comparisons, and global coordination.

The empirical results are promising. On HotpotQA, the strongest variant improves substantially over the unoptimized MAS and outperforms MAPPO; transfer results on 2WikiMultihopQA and MuSiQue suggest that the learned behavior is not entirely dataset-specific.

The paper includes several informative analyses: role-wise training ablations, final-only versus composite rewards, reward-aggregation alternatives, group-size sensitivity, learning curves, resource measurements, and agent-behavior diagnostics.
The presentation is generally clear, with concrete prompts, hardware information, principal hyperparameters, and pseudocode supplied in the appendix.
weaknesses: A central reproducibility inconsistency remains: Algorithm 5 assigns one group identifier to all agent outputs within a trajectory, whereas the method description and Proposition 3 describe per-agent groups containing outputs across trajectories. These constructions produce different normalization sets and potentially different updates; the implemented procedure must be stated unambiguously.

The theoretical contribution is weaker than advertised. The claimed equivalence relies on a strong context-sufficiency assumption and constructs a transcript version that uses the same per-agent grouping as MHGPO, rather than standard transcript-level GRPO. It establishes a largely expected per-token correspondence, but does not justify why heterogeneous normalization is unbiased or stable when the assumption fails. Equal role-wise averaging in Equation 6 also need not equal ordinary transcript-level objective weighting.

The experiments do not cleanly isolate the benefit of heterogeneous grouping. FoF, RR, and IS alter sampling distributions, rollout budgets, and group composition simultaneously. The role-freezing ablation shows that joint training matters, but does not establish that the proposed grouping mechanism captures inter-agent dependencies. An equal-rollout-budget comparison using identical trajectories but alternative normalization groups is needed.

Uncertainty is missing for the main comparison in Table 1 despite several reported gains being small. Three-seed results appear only for selected ablations, and there are no statistical tests. Consequently, the consistency of improvements over MAPPO—especially out of domain—is not fully established.

Several implementation and evaluation details required for reproduction are underspecified, including evaluation-set sizes, decoding parameters, retrieval depth and corpus snapshot, snippet construction, PPO epoch count, exact format-penalty thresholds such as the Answerer length cutoff, and the nonstandard 'Accuracy' calculation. No code or trained artifacts are identified.

The efficiency comparison favors MHGPO partly because MAPPO uses an entire 8B critic. That is a legitimate implementation, but comparison with a value head, smaller critic, or parameter-efficient critic would better support the broader efficiency claim. Percent memory and per-step time are also difficult to interpret across methods with different rollout workloads.

Generality is limited to one shared 8B backbone, one fixed three-stage linear RAG architecture, and QA datasets. Claims of applicability to broader multi-agent systems, larger teams, or nonlinear interaction graphs are therefore prospective rather than empirically supported. Overall, the contribution appears suitable for Findings, but the evidence and specification are not yet strong enough for a main-conference recommendation.
